title: The Context Window Problem — Why Agents "Forget"

The far side is an avalanche of papers: error logs, file printouts, reasoning chains, tool outputs, conversation transcripts, all piling up and burying the original plan documents. panels.speaker: DISCBOT

panels.text: A context window is the maximum amount of text a language model can process in a single interaction. Think of it as the model's working memory — everything it can “see” at once. If information is outside the window, the model cannot access it. It is gone.

panels.text: That sounds enormous. Surely 200,000 tokens is enough? Not quite. And the reason is a subtle, well-documented phenomenon that researchers call “Lost in the Middle.”

panels.prompt: A three-panel horizontal comic strip sequence showing context degradation. Left panel: 'Minute 0' label, a clean fresh notebook with a crisp plan visible (Step 1: Fix auth, Step 2: Add tests, Step 3: Update docs), everything clear and legible, bright lighting. Center panel: 'Minute 30' label, the same notebook now buried under a massive pile of printed code, error logs, and file contents, the plan barely peeking out from underneath, dimmer lighting. Right panel: 'Minute 45' label, the agent writing 'First let me fix the authentication...' on a new page, not realizing it already completed that step, a faded completed checkmark barely visible behind the pile, confused atmosphere. Comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes, violet tinting increasing with each panel

panels.text: For a coding agent, this creates a slow-motion disaster. The agent starts with a clean, clear context. But as it works — reading files, running commands, analyzing errors — the context fills up. The original plan slides into the foggy middle. The agent may re-do work it already completed, contradict earlier decisions, or “forget” critical constraints.

A context window is like a desk. A bigger desk lets you spread out more documents. But no matter how big the desk, the papers in the center tend to get buried. Making the window bigger does not fix the problem. The issue is not the size of the memory — it is how attention distributes across it.

A white speech bubble with black outline above. Inside the bubble the text reads: "Not a sudden explosion. A slow, quiet accumulation." panels.text: Context degradation was a serious problem. But there was another challenge agents faced — one that actually showcased their most impressive capability. What happens when the code they write... does not work?
